# Aqueous equilibrium notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Within water at ambient conditions, increasing total acid concentration should lower pH and reduce the free deprotonated fraction, as expected for a weak monoprotic acid. The two supplied reference assays at ~7.5–8 µM are mutually consistent and show high dissociation (~0.78) with no precipitation.

## H2 [tentative]
A precipitation threshold may appear only at sufficiently high total loading; above it, precipitation_signal should rise while dissolved speciation/pH may become buffered or show a change in slope.

## Design commitment
Use 12 independent ambient-water batches spanning concentration by varying both amount and volume. Include concentration-matched pairs at different amounts/volumes to distinguish concentration control from total-amount or vessel-volume effects, plus repeats near any discovered threshold. Intermediate pH-meter readings will be used in each batch as noisier cross-checks; final assays are authoritative anchors. Evidence will be interpreted relative to stated assay noise, and mechanistic alternatives (activity effects, solubility-limited acid, amount/volume artifacts) will remain distinct.

# Aqueous equilibrium notebook

## H1 [supported over dilute-to-0.05 M water; functional form unresolved]
Increasing analytical concentration lowers pH and free deprotonated fraction. Final assays span approximately: 10 µM, pH_norm 0.361 and alpha 0.741 (runner-operation-0005); 0.001 M, 0.275 and 0.140 (runner-operation-0010); 0.01 M, 0.237 and 0.056 (runner-operation-0015); 0.05 M, 0.209 and 0.014 (runner-operation-0020). The monotone changes are much larger than final-assay noise. A simple weak-monoprotic-acid model is plausible, but activity/concentration corrections can be observationally equivalent.

## H2 [unresolved]
No convincing precipitation has yet appeared through 0.05 M: final signals are 0–0.011, near the 0.006 channel noise. Intermediate pH-meter precipitation estimates are too noisy to establish small effects. Prediction made now: if a threshold lies above 0.05 M, subsequent 0.1–0.67 M batches should show a final precipitation_signal clearly separated from this near-zero band; otherwise H2 will be shelved.

## H3 [to test]
At matched analytical concentration, pH/dissociation/precipitation depend primarily on n/V, not total moles or volume. Planned 0.1 M and 0.5 M matched pairs test this; systematic differences beyond assay scatter would favor amount/volume dependence or an unmodeled vessel effect.

## Scope/confounds
All claims are ambient-water equilibrium observations. pH-meter/final-assay differences are not treated as time evolution because the instruments have unequal noise and the final sample is destructive; final assays are primary.

# Aqueous equilibrium notebook — final source-stage interpretation

## H1 [supported in ambient water, 10 µM–0.67 M]
Analytical concentration is the dominant effective control variable. As C=n/V increases, final pH_norm falls monotonically from 0.361 at 10 µM (runner-operation-0005) to 0.089 at 0.67 M (runner-operation-0040), and the free deprotonated fraction falls from 0.741 to values indistinguishable from zero at high loading. The two supplied ~8 µM references (alpha ~0.78, no precipitation) agree with this dilute trend.

For the four lowest autonomous concentrations (10 µM–0.05 M), combining final pH and alpha with an ideal monoprotic-acid identity gives effective pKa estimates 4.59, 4.64, 4.55, and 4.76. Thus an effective pKa near 4.6 is a compact local description, not a uniquely identified thermodynamic mechanism; activity effects, assay noise (especially alpha near zero), and precipitation limit its extrapolation.

## H2 [supported as a gradual high-loading response; sharp threshold rejected]
Final precipitation_signal is near zero through 0.05 M (runner-operation-0020), then rises across 0.1 M (~0.021–0.031 across runner-operation-0025, -0045, -0050), 0.2 M (0.057; runner-operation-0030), 0.4 M (0.076; runner-operation-0035), 0.5 M (0.091–0.098; runner-operation-0055, -0060), and 0.67 M (0.102; runner-operation-0040). Changes across the broad range exceed 0.006 assay noise, but the data support a smooth bounded proxy more clearly than a sharp solubility threshold. Equivalent explanations include true precipitation controlled by dissolved neutral acid, an empirical concentration response with saturation, or coupled activity/solubility effects; public channels do not identify solid composition.

## H3 [supported at tested matched concentrations; small scale effects unresolved]
Matched n/V tests support concentration rather than total amount or liquid volume as the main predictor. At 0.1 M, three scales (0.003/0.03, 0.006/0.06, 0.008/0.08 mol/L) have final pH_norm 0.172–0.174, alpha 0.0068–0.0095, and precipitation 0.021–0.031 (runner-operation-0025, -0045, -0050). At 0.5 M, 0.020/0.040 and 0.040/0.080 pairs agree closely in pH_norm (~0.0955–0.0959) and alpha (~0.004–0.006), with precipitation 0.091 versus 0.098 (runner-operation-0055, -0060). Differences are numerical but not compelling evidence of a scale effect given stated per-assay noise and absence of extensive replication.

## Measurement and scope decisions
Final assays are primary because their declared noise is lower. Intermediate pH-meter observations broadly reproduce the concentration ordering but individual alpha/precipitation discrepancies are compatible with their larger noise, so they do not establish temporal drift. Conclusions apply only to ambient water, the anonymous acid feed, and this bounded loading range; solvent, temperature, kinetics, solid identity, and ionic-strength mechanisms were not independently varied.

## Evidentiary-anchor decision
Batch 10 (runner-operation-0046 through -0050; 0.008 mol in 0.08 L, 0.1 M) is a useful anchor: it lies at the onset region where precipitation is distinguishable from the dilute baseline, has non-boundary volume/amount, and participates in the three-scale matched-concentration comparison. This choice is for interpretability, not optimization.

K1.report:
Scientific account of the bounded aqueous-equilibrium world

1. Public background and definitions

The public task defines pH_normalized = pH/14, acid_dissociation_fraction as the free deprotonated-acid fraction relative to total acid feed, and precipitation_signal as the precipitated-acid fraction relative to total acid feed. The setting is explicitly a bounded weak-acid/precipitation slice, not a model of general aqueous chemistry. Materials other than water and the anonymous limiting reagent have no task-specific chemical identity that can support a molecular assignment. No explicit archival equation or fitted local relationship was supplied.

The final-assay standard deviations relevant here are 0.002 for pH_normalized, 0.006 for acid_dissociation_fraction, and 0.006 for precipitation_signal. Thus the corresponding nominal pH uncertainty is about 0.028 pH unit. Intermediate pH-meter channels have larger declared noise and were treated as secondary checks. The public equilibrium_confidence channel is an environment diagnostic, not my scientific confidence.

Two public preliminary assays used 0.6 micromol of reagent in 0.080 and 0.075 L of water, corresponding to 7.5 and 8.0 micromolar. They reported pH_normalized 0.37469 and 0.37497, dissociation fractions 0.78044 and 0.78302, and zero precipitation signal. These are public background observations rather than my campaign batches.

2. Experimental design and actual observations

I completed 12 independent ambient-water batches. The analytical loading C was defined as added reagent amount divided by initial liquid volume. Each batch received an intermediate pH-meter measurement and a post-termination final assay. The following are the actual final-assay observations:

- Batch 1: 0.0000006 mol in 0.060 L, C = 0.000010 M. pH_normalized = 0.36080 (pH about 5.051), dissociation fraction = 0.74109, precipitation signal = 0.00116.
- Batch 2: 0.000060 mol in 0.060 L, C = 0.001 M. pH_normalized = 0.27476 (pH about 3.847), dissociation fraction = 0.13965, precipitation signal = 0.00569.
- Batch 3: 0.00060 mol in 0.060 L, C = 0.010 M. pH_normalized = 0.23749 (pH about 3.325), dissociation fraction = 0.05591, precipitation signal = 0.
- Batch 4: 0.0030 mol in 0.060 L, C = 0.050 M. pH_normalized = 0.20896 (pH about 2.925), dissociation fraction = 0.01437, precipitation signal = 0.01073.
- Batch 5: 0.0060 mol in 0.060 L, C = 0.100 M. pH_normalized = 0.17124 (pH about 2.397), dissociation fraction = 0.00950, precipitation signal = 0.02140.
- Batch 6: 0.012 mol in 0.060 L, C = 0.200 M. pH_normalized = 0.13658 (pH about 1.912), dissociation fraction = 0, precipitation signal = 0.05678.
- Batch 7: 0.024 mol in 0.060 L, C = 0.400 M. pH_normalized = 0.10298 (pH about 1.442), dissociation fraction = 0, precipitation signal = 0.07590.
- Batch 8: 0.040 mol in 0.060 L, C = 0.667 M. pH_normalized = 0.08893 (pH about 1.245), dissociation fraction = 0.00216, precipitation signal = 0.10238.
- Batch 9: 0.0030 mol in 0.030 L, C = 0.100 M. pH_normalized = 0.17160 (pH about 2.402), dissociation fraction = 0.00676, precipitation signal = 0.02893.
- Batch 10: 0.0080 mol in 0.080 L, C = 0.100 M. pH_normalized = 0.17430 (pH about 2.440), dissociation fraction = 0.00856, precipitation signal = 0.03077.
- Batch 11: 0.020 mol in 0.040 L, C = 0.500 M. pH_normalized = 0.09552 (pH about 1.337), dissociation fraction = 0.00567, precipitation signal = 0.09051.
- Batch 12: 0.040 mol in 0.080 L, C = 0.500 M. pH_normalized = 0.09592 (pH about 1.343), dissociation fraction = 0.00438, precipitation signal = 0.09759.

Intermediate pH-meter observations broadly reproduced the ordering with concentration. Their occasional nonzero dissociation estimates where final assays returned zero, and their noisier precipitation estimates at low loading, are consistent with their larger declared uncertainties; I do not interpret those discrepancies as temporal evolution.

3. Supported empirical relationships

Loading and pH: Across the fixed-volume 0.060 L sequence, increasing C from 0.000010 to 0.667 M lowered pH_normalized monotonically from 0.3608 to 0.0889. The associated pH fell from about 5.05 to 1.25. These changes greatly exceed assay uncertainty. Within the tested ambient-water domain, greater loading therefore robustly produces a more acidic liquid.

Loading and dissociation: The free deprotonated fraction fell from 0.741 at 0.000010 M to 0.140 at 0.001 M, 0.0559 at 0.010 M, and 0.0144 at 0.050 M. At 0.1 M and above it was roughly 0–0.01, comparable to the 0.006 assay noise and bounded below by zero. The supported conclusion is a strong decline in fractional dissociation with concentration; exact high-loading fractions are poorly resolved.

Dilution and scale: Concentration-matched batches distinguish n/V from total moles or absolute volume. At 0.100 M, batches 5, 9, and 10 used 0.030, 0.060, and 0.080 L and different total amounts. Their pH_normalized values were 0.1712–0.1743, dissociation fractions 0.0068–0.0095, and precipitation signals 0.0214–0.0308. At 0.500 M, batches 11 and 12 differed twofold in both amount and volume but gave pH_normalized 0.09552 and 0.09592, dissociation fractions 0.00567 and 0.00438, and precipitation signals 0.09051 and 0.09759. These comparisons support C = n/V as the dominant effective variable. The small numerical differences do not compellingly establish an independent amount or volume effect given assay noise and limited replication.

Precipitation: The signal remained at or near the noise floor through 0.050 M, then increased over the high-loading series: about 0.021–0.031 at 0.100 M, 0.0568 at 0.200 M, 0.0759 at 0.400 M, 0.0905–0.0976 at 0.500 M, and 0.1024 at 0.667 M. This is evidence for a gradual, bounded concentration-dependent precipitation response. The observations do not locate a sharp threshold. A practical onset region is roughly 0.05–0.1 M, but that wording describes detectability, not a proven phase boundary.

4. Effective acid-dissociation relationship

As an inference, not a directly supplied law, I tested the ideal monoprotic-acid expression

Ka,eff = [H+] alpha/(1-alpha), with [H+] = 10^(-pH),

where alpha is the measured free deprotonated fraction. Batches 1–4 give effective pKa values of approximately 4.59, 4.64, 4.55, and 4.76. Thus pKa,eff near 4.6 is a useful compact local description from about 0.000010 to 0.010 M, and is still roughly compatible at 0.050 M. The first three estimates agree closely despite a 1000-fold concentration span and also align qualitatively with the two public dilute reference assays.

This calculation does not establish a unique thermodynamic Ka. At 0.050 M the dissociation fraction is already only about twice its assay standard deviation; at higher concentrations it is frequently clipped at zero or dominated by measurement noise. Activities, precipitation, ionic-strength effects, and any unobserved dissolved forms can all make an apparent Ka concentration-dependent. Accordingly, pKa about 4.6 should be used as a dilute-range effective parameter, not extrapolated as an exact invariant across the full range.

5. Interpretation of precipitation coupling

The observations show correlation among increasing C, falling pH, falling fractional dissociation, and rising precipitation signal. They do not reveal which dissolved form precipitates or whether precipitation causally controls pH. Several explanations remain observationally compatible:

- A conventional weak monoprotic acid has decreasing fractional dissociation as concentration rises, while a neutral or ion-paired form separately approaches a solubility limit.
- A deprotonated salt or another coupled species precipitates, with activity coefficients changing at high loading.
- The precipitation channel is an empirical saturating function of analytical concentration rather than evidence for a single sharp solubility product.
- Nonideal aqueous activities jointly alter pH, apparent dissociation, and the precipitation proxy without a simple two-species mass-action description.

The smooth rise and apparent flattening of precipitation_signal toward about 0.1 within the observed range are compatible with a saturating empirical response, but neither its asymptote nor a functional form is identified. Because the proxy is normalized to total acid feed and bounded, it must not be interpreted directly as a precipitate concentration or universal solubility.

6. Uncertainty and limitations

Most concentrations have only one final assay. The matched 0.1 M triplet and 0.5 M pair provide limited reproducibility/scale information but are not extensive replication. Individual precipitation signals below roughly 0.01 and individual dissociation fractions near zero should be regarded as poorly separated from the measurement floor. The monotone pH trend and the large overall changes in dissociation and precipitation are much more secure than fine differences between neighboring high-loading batches.

Final equilibrium_residual values were small, from zero to about 0.0069, so no batch displayed a large diagnostic residual. Final equilibrium_confidence varied rather than remaining uniformly high; it was about 0.45 in the most dilute batch, reached about 0.81 near 0.01 M, and was about 0.66–0.72 through much of the high-loading region. These are environment diagnostics and are not substituted for inferential confidence.

All autonomous batches used water near ambient conditions. Solvent identity, temperature, added electrolyte, catalyst, atmosphere, equilibration time, solid composition, and explicit ionic strength were not independently varied. Consequently, the supported scope is the anonymous acid feed in ambient water from approximately 0.000010 to 0.667 M, with liquid volumes of 0.030–0.080 L. Claims about other solvents, temperatures, named acids, microscopic species, true phase equilibria, or behavior outside this range would be conjecture.

7. Overall conclusion

Within this bounded world, analytical loading n/V is the best-supported effective control variable. Dilution raises pH and increases the free deprotonated fraction; concentration lowers both and progressively increases the public precipitation proxy. A dilute-range weak-monoprotic-acid model with effective pKa around 4.6 summarizes the pH/dissociation relationship, while precipitation becomes clearly important above roughly 0.05–0.1 M and rises smoothly to about 0.10 by 0.67 M. Matched-concentration tests argue against a large independent effect of total moles or volume over 0.030–0.080 L, though small scale effects remain unresolved. The data identify effective relationships, not a unique molecular mechanism or a sharp solubility law.

The dilute effective-acid relationship supports an intermediate dissociation fraction. No resolved precipitation was observed in this region, so the bounded interval includes zero.

The dissociation measurement was clipped at zero there, but nearby data support a small nonnegative latent fraction. Intervals account for assay noise, model uncertainty, and the smaller volume.

The very small 0.010 L volume is an extrapolation beyond the observed scale range, so these are the widest intervals among the 0.600 M predictions. Q.rationale: Predictions use the sealed account's principal inference that analytical concentration n/V dominates over total amount and volume in ambient water. pH and dissociation were interpolated primarily on log concentration; the dilute dissociation estimates were also constrained by the effective monoprotic-acid relationship with pKa near 4.6. Precipitation was modeled as a gradual bounded response rising above the 0.05–0.1 M region, without imposing a sharp threshold. The 80% intervals combine declared final-assay noise with interpolation uncertainty, limited replication, near-zero clipping, extrapolation to 0.010–0.020 L volumes, and untested addition-path effects. Identical final concentrations receive common central predictions, while scale and staged-path cases receive different uncertainty widths.

K2.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested relationships

Supported: In ambient water over the observed 0.000010–0.667 M range, analytical concentration n/V was the dominant effective predictor. Increasing concentration lowered pH and the free deprotonated fraction. The dilute observations were approximately consistent with an effective monoprotic-acid pKa near 4.6. The precipitation proxy was near its measurement floor through roughly 0.05 M and increased progressively at higher loading. Matched-concentration batches at 0.1 M and 0.5 M supported concentration control over any large independent effect of total amount or volume within 0.030–0.080 L.

Contradicted or weakened: A sharp precipitation threshold was not supported. Batches 4–8 instead showed a gradual rise from precipitation_signal 0.0107 at 0.05 M to 0.0214 at 0.1 M, 0.0568 at 0.2 M, and 0.1024 at 0.667 M. A single invariant ideal Ka across the entire range was also not justified because dissociation approached the assay floor and nonideality or precipitation became important.

Untested: Addition-order and hysteresis effects, equilibration kinetics, temperature dependence, other solvents, ionic-strength manipulation, redissolution after dilution, solid identity, and behavior outside the observed concentration and volume ranges were not tested. Small scale effects remain unresolved even though large ones were not evident.

2. Observations that changed the account

There were actual observations that changed the developing account. The early batches established the strong decline in pH and dissociation with concentration. Batches 5–8 changed the initial tentative precipitation-threshold idea: rather than revealing a sharp transition, they showed a smooth high-loading increase. Batches 9 and 10, compared with batch 5 at the same 0.1 M concentration, and batches 11 and 12 at 0.5 M, strengthened the interpretation that n/V mattered more than absolute amount or volume. No new observations, prediction outcomes, or scores have been provided since K1 and Q were sealed.

3. Competing explanations

Some alternatives are partly distinguishable. The matched-scale data disfavor a large pure-total-amount or pure-volume effect relative to concentration. The monotone dilute response is compatible with weak-acid mass action and is less compatible with a concentration-independent dissociation fraction.

Important mechanistic alternatives remain unresolved. The apparent pKa may represent an ideal monoprotic acid, concentration-dependent activities, ion pairing, or other hidden dissolved forms. The precipitation proxy could arise from neutral-acid precipitation, precipitation of an ionic or paired form, or an empirical bounded concentration response. The data do not identify the solid, a solubility product, or whether precipitation causally modifies pH. Smooth saturation and a broad distribution of microscopic precipitation thresholds are also observationally equivalent over the measured range.

4. Next single legal experiment

I would prepare 0.030 L water, add 0.012 mol reagent to create a temporary 0.4 M state, then add another 0.030 L water to reach a final 0.2 M state, terminate, and measure with the final assay. This is legally within the published per-operation bounds and can be compared with batch 6, which reached 0.2 M without first visiting 0.4 M.

If equilibrium is path independent and dilution permits complete redissolution, the result should resemble batch 6: pH_normalized about 0.137, near-zero resolved dissociation, and precipitation_signal about 0.057 within measurement and model uncertainty. A substantially larger precipitation signal after the high-concentration excursion would support persistent solids, hysteresis, or slow redissolution. Convergence only after an added wait would suggest kinetics rather than a different equilibrium. A lower signal or altered pH without corresponding precipitation persistence would suggest dilution/order-dependent activity or operational effects. One experiment would be diagnostic but would still require replication.

5. Evidentiary limits

The characterization rests on 12 autonomous final assays plus two public dilute reference assays. Most concentrations were measured once. The matched-concentration groups provide limited scale checks but not extensive replication. Final-assay noise is especially consequential for dissociation fractions near zero and precipitation signals below about 0.01. Zero-valued fractions may reflect bounded noisy estimates rather than exactly zero chemistry.

Only water near ambient conditions was studied. No direct composition, solid-phase identity, activity coefficient, ionic strength, kinetic trajectory, or true dissolved concentration was measured. precipitation_signal is a bounded normalized proxy, not a precipitate concentration. Consequently, the evidence supports effective relationships but not a unique molecular mechanism or thermodynamic phase law.

6. Least reliable Q forecasts

Q08 and Q11 are least reliable because their 0.010 L volumes lie below every autonomous observed volume. Q09 and Q10 are also weak because their staged or reordered paths were never experimentally tested; their common central predictions assume path-independent equilibrium. Q01–Q06 use 0.020 L, also below the observed 0.030–0.080 L range, although their concentrations are mostly interpolations within the observed loading domain.

Metric-specific reliability also varies. High-loading acid-dissociation forecasts are weak because the observed values were comparable to noise and sometimes clipped at zero. Precipitation forecasts near 0.05–0.1 M are sensitive to the unresolved shape of the onset region. The central forecasts for Q09 and Q10 were not logically inconsistent with K1, but they extend its scope by assuming path independence; their widened intervals acknowledged rather than resolved that extrapolation.

7. Limits on generalization

New loading: Interpolation within 0.000010–0.667 M is more defensible than extrapolation. Above 0.667 M, neither the precipitation asymptote nor continued pH behavior is established. Below the public micromolar references, water background and assay limitations could dominate.

New dilution or scale: Concentration equivalence was observed only over 0.030–0.080 L. Surface-to-volume effects, sampling fractions, nucleation probability, or container effects could become important at smaller or larger scales.

New paths: The campaign used simple solvent-then-reagent preparation. Staging, temporary supersaturation, reverse addition, waiting, heating, or dilution after precipitation may produce hysteresis or kinetic differences that the final-state model cannot predict securely.

New worlds: The reagent and mechanisms are anonymous and world-specific. The effective pKa and precipitation curve cannot be transferred to a named acid, another solvent, temperature, electrolyte background, or real laboratory material. Generalization is therefore limited to this bounded synthetic world and the tested ambient-water regime.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative; prediction before autonomous experiments]
For water-only batches near ambient conditions, increasing total acid loading at fixed liquid volume should lower pH and the free deprotonated fraction. Dilution at fixed acid amount should raise both. A precipitation proxy may remain near zero at low concentration and appear nonlinearly above a concentration/loading threshold. Equivalent effective explanations include concentration-dependent weak-acid mass action, activity-coefficient changes, and removal of neutral/deprotonated material by a solubility limit; these are not yet distinguishable.

**Planned test.** Use a 3 x 4 endpoint grid of acid amount (approximately 6e-7, 0.006, 0.030 mol) and water volume (0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08 L), with a pH-meter observation at half the endpoint loading and a final assay after the second addition. Replicate-like overlap and supplied references R01/R02 will help assess noise. I will treat differences cautiously relative to stated channel noise and will revise the grid interpretation if staged addition shows unexpected directionality.

**Scope.** Anonymous acid in the bounded benchmark, water, near initial ambient temperature; no claim yet about named chemistry or other solvents.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in the low-loading water scope]
At total acid feed 6e-7 mol, dilution from 0.02 to 0.08 L raises pH_normalized and free dissociation. Final assays span pH_normalized about 0.342 to 0.375 and dissociation about 0.545 to 0.790 (runner-operation-0006, -0012, -0018, -0024). The 0.08 L endpoint agrees closely with supplied R01/R02, while staged half-load pH-meter readings have the same directional pattern (runner-operation-0003, -0009, -0015, -0021). This supports concentration dependence rather than total moles alone in this range.

Small nonzero precipitation readings at very low loading are inconsistent across instruments/endpoints and comparable to stated measurement noise, so precipitation is treated as zero/unresolved here rather than evidence of a physical precipitate.

## H2 [tentative; prediction before higher-load tests]
If a simple weak-acid concentration relationship dominates before precipitation, raising feed concentration should lower pH and dissociation smoothly. If a solubility constraint appears, precipitation should rise nonlinearly and may decouple pH/dissociation from nominal total feed. The upcoming 0.006 and 0.030 mol grids test this; repeated concentrations created by different amount-volume combinations can distinguish concentration control from an independent total-loading or volume effect.

**Scope and alternatives.** Water-only, near ambient temperature. Effective concentration dependence could represent mass action, activities, or concentration-dependent association. Precipitation mechanism and solid identity remain unidentifiable from these channels alone.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested water/ambient scope]
Nominal analytical concentration C = total acid feed / liquid volume is the dominant effective coordinate for pH across the tested endpoint grid. At each fixed feed, dilution raises pH_normalized (runner-operation-0006 to -0024; -0030 to -0048; -0054 to -0072). Descriptive least-squares fits of pH_normalized versus ln(C) have slopes -0.0236 at 7.5e-6 to 3e-5 M, -0.0247 at 0.075 to 0.30 M, and -0.0399 at 0.375 to 1.5 M. These are summaries, not a claimed universal law; the high-concentration segment is steeper and there is a large unsampled concentration gap.

The free deprotonated fraction likewise decreases strongly with concentration: final-assay values are about 0.545-0.790 in the micromolar grid (runner-operation-0006, -0012, -0018, -0024), but are at or near the zero boundary in the 0.075-1.5 M grids (runner-operation-0030 through -0072). Because many readings are clipped/noise-scale near zero, the data identify a collapse in free fraction, not its precise functional form.

## H2 [supported threshold-like precipitation proxy; mechanism unresolved]
Endpoint precipitation is indistinguishable from zero through 0.50 M, then rises to 0.034 at 0.75 M and 0.080 at 1.5 M (runner-operation-0066, -0060, -0054; final-assay channel SD 0.006). Thus a threshold-like onset between roughly 0.5 and 0.75 M is supported for these endpoint conditions. The staged pH-meter precipitation values have SD 0.02 and mostly remain noise-scale, so they do not finely locate onset.

A solubility limit is a parsimonious effective explanation, but precipitation_signal alone cannot identify which acid form precipitates, solid stoichiometry, nucleation kinetics, or whether high-concentration nonideality/association produces an equivalent bounded response. The concurrent steeper pH-concentration slope above 0.5 M is consistent with coupling but does not establish causation.

## H3 [unresolved total-loading/volume effects]
The grid strongly establishes dilution trends, but exact concentration-matched comparisons often use different instruments/stages (for example 0.75 M at runner-operation-0057 versus -0060). Instrument noise and staged-history differences confound a strict proof that C alone is sufficient. A future decisive test would use final assays at the same C with several total amounts/volumes and replication near 0.5-0.8 M.

## Decision and scope
Use batch 9 (0.030 mol in 0.020 L; runner-operation-0054) as the evidentiary anchor because it cleanly demonstrates the high-concentration regime and the strongest precipitation signal, while the rest of the grid supplies its contrast. Claims apply only to this anonymous bounded acid in water near ambient initial conditions; they do not establish named chemistry, temperature effects, or behavior in other solvents. Supplied R01/R02 and batch 4 agree at 6e-7 mol in 0.08 L, supporting repeatability at the dilute endpoint.

K1.report:
## 1. Public background

This is a bounded synthetic weak-acid/precipitation benchmark, not a model of general aqueous chemistry or an identified real acid. The reagent and mechanism-to-species mapping are anonymous, and no task-specific material dossier or prior local law was supplied. Water was the only solvent tested. The public definitions are: pH_normalized = pH/14; acid_dissociation_fraction = free deprotonated acid divided by total acid feed; precipitation_signal = precipitated acid divided by total acid feed. The stated final-assay standard deviations are 0.002 for pH_normalized, 0.006 for dissociation, and 0.006 for precipitation. Corresponding pH-meter standard deviations are 0.004, 0.015, and 0.020. Equilibrium_confidence is an environment diagnostic, not scientific confidence.

Two supplied preliminary final assays were actual public observations: 6e-7 mol in 0.080 L gave pH_normalized 0.374645, dissociation 0.774900, and precipitation 0; 6e-7 mol in 0.075 L gave 0.374918, 0.777236, and 0.

## 2. Experiments and actual observations

I completed 12 water batches near ambient temperature. Endpoint feed amounts were 6e-7, 0.006, or 0.030 mol, each crossed with liquid volumes of 0.020, 0.040, 0.060, and 0.080 L. In every batch, a pH-meter measurement was taken after half of the final feed had been added, followed by the second addition, termination, and a final assay. The final-assay endpoints are the primary comparable dataset:

| Batch | Feed (mol) | Volume (L) | Nominal C (mol/L) | pH_normalized | pH | Dissociation fraction | Precipitation signal |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 6e-7 | 0.020 | 3.0e-5 | 0.341788 | 4.785 | 0.544694 | 0.000643 |
| 2 | 6e-7 | 0.040 | 1.5e-5 | 0.356810 | 4.995 | 0.663268 | 0 |
| 3 | 6e-7 | 0.060 | 1.0e-5 | 0.366780 | 5.135 | 0.747505 | 0 |
| 4 | 6e-7 | 0.080 | 7.5e-6 | 0.374690 | 5.246 | 0.790026 | 0.003290 |
| 5 | 0.006 | 0.020 | 0.300 | 0.114640 | 1.605 | 0.000395 | 0.002269 |
| 6 | 0.006 | 0.040 | 0.150 | 0.131966 | 1.848 | 0.006344 | 0 |
| 7 | 0.006 | 0.060 | 0.100 | 0.139855 | 1.958 | 0 | 0.000441 |
| 8 | 0.006 | 0.080 | 0.075 | 0.149990 | 2.100 | 0.012572 | 0 |
| 9 | 0.030 | 0.020 | 1.500 | 0.051536 | 0.722 | 0.007898 | 0.080351 |
| 10 | 0.030 | 0.040 | 0.750 | 0.074664 | 1.045 | 0 | 0.034245 |
| 11 | 0.030 | 0.060 | 0.500 | 0.096772 | 1.355 | 0.001252 | 0.000232 |
| 12 | 0.030 | 0.080 | 0.375 | 0.105443 | 1.476 | 0 | 0.002823 |

Batch 4 closely reproduced the supplied dilute reference pH and broadly reproduced its dissociation fraction. The intermediate half-loading measurements independently showed the same dilution direction for pH. For example, batches 1–4 at half loading ranged from pH_normalized 0.3503 at 0.020 L to 0.3939 at 0.080 L, while dissociation rose from 0.662 to 0.883. Intermediate precipitation estimates were mostly noise-scale under the less precise pH-meter channel.

## 3. Supported empirical relationships

**Loading, volume, and pH.** At every fixed final amount, increasing water volume raised pH; equivalently, increasing nominal concentration lowered pH. Thus concentration or dilution is a strongly supported effective coordinate. Descriptive least-squares fits of pH_normalized against ln(C) had slopes of -0.0236 over 7.5e-6–3.0e-5 M, -0.0247 over 0.075–0.300 M, and -0.0399 over 0.375–1.50 M. These correspond to approximate pH changes of -0.76, -0.80, and -1.29 per tenfold concentration increase. The steeper high-concentration segment suggests curvature or a regime change; these fits are summaries rather than universal laws. There is a large unmeasured gap between 3e-5 and 0.075 M.

**Acid dissociation.** In the dilute final-assay range, dissociation increased monotonically with dilution, from 0.545 at 3e-5 M to 0.790 at 7.5e-6 M. In the 0.075–1.50 M endpoints it was at or very near the zero boundary, with all values no greater than 0.0126. This supports a large concentration-dependent collapse in the reported free deprotonated fraction. It does not resolve the detailed functional form because most concentrated results are comparable to the 0.006 final-assay uncertainty and some are clipped at zero.

**Precipitation.** Final-assay precipitation was indistinguishable from zero through 0.50 M. It then rose to 0.0342 at 0.75 M and 0.0804 at 1.50 M, well above the 0.006 channel standard deviation. Under these endpoint conditions, the observations therefore support a threshold-like onset between approximately 0.50 and 0.75 M, followed by a larger response with concentration. Batch 9 provides the clearest high-concentration anchor. The threshold is a statement about the normalized public proxy, not proof of a particular solid phase.

## 4. Inference versus conjecture

The inference most directly supported by the grid is that nominal concentration, rather than total moles alone, organizes pH and dilute dissociation behavior. However, concentration was produced by varying volume at fixed amount within each four-batch block. Exact concentration-matched final assays using independently varied amount and volume were not performed, so an additional total-loading or volume effect is not excluded.

A weak-acid mass-action picture is qualitatively compatible with higher dissociation on dilution. A simple ideal monoprotic model with one fixed dissociation constant is not established across the whole range: the reported dissociation nearly vanishes at moderate and high loading while pH remains strongly acidic, and the pH-concentration slope steepens in the highest range. Plausible competing effective explanations include concentration-dependent activity coefficients, association or oligomerization, an unobserved background electrolyte/proton reservoir, or coupling to precipitation. The public channels cannot distinguish these explanations or identify species.

A solubility-limit interpretation is a parsimonious conjecture for the precipitation onset. Alternatives include a bounded proxy responding to high-concentration association, nonideal phase behavior, or a nucleation/history effect. The coincidence of stronger precipitation and a steeper pH trend above roughly 0.5 M is consistent with coupling, but does not prove that precipitation causes the pH change or identify whether neutral or ionized acid precipitates.

## 5. Uncertainty, limitations, and scope

All autonomous endpoints were single final assays; the supplied dilute references provide only limited repeatability evidence. With the stated final-assay uncertainties, precipitation values below about 0.003 in batches 1–8 and 11–12 should be treated as zero/noise-scale, whereas batches 9 and 10 are clear positive signals. Concentrated dissociation values are poorly resolved because they lie near the lower bound. pH trends are much larger than the stated 0.002 normalized uncertainty and are consequently the most robust relationship.

No temperature series, equilibration-time series, other solvents, catalysts, electrolyte profiles, solid characterization, or direct species measurements were performed. The equilibrium diagnostic residuals were generally near zero, but that is an environment diagnostic and does not validate a chemical mechanism. Conclusions apply only to this anonymous bounded acid in water, near the tested ambient conditions, over the sampled concentration ranges. The most informative future tests would replicate final assays around 0.5–0.8 M, test several amount-volume pairs at identical concentration, and fill the wide 3e-5–0.075 M gap.

predictions.rationale: At 0.002 M this batch lies in the large unsampled gap between the dilute and bulk observations. A concentration-based weak-acid interpolation predicts partial dissociation and pH between the two observed regimes. It is far below the observed precipitation onset, so the precipitation estimate is effectively zero; the interval is widened for interpolation uncertainty.

At 0.006 M, increased concentration should lower both pH and free dissociation relative to Q01. The point estimate follows the effective concentration relationship inferred from the dilute dissociation data and the transition toward the 0.075 M observations. No precipitation was supported anywhere near this concentration.

The 0.020 M endpoint remains in the unmeasured concentration gap, so model uncertainty dominates instrumental uncertainty. The inferred weak-acid relationship gives a small but resolved free fraction, while the pH trend continues downward approximately with log concentration. Precipitation remains effectively absent.

At 0.060 M this condition is close to the lowest observed bulk concentration, 0.075 M, making the pH interpolation comparatively well constrained. Dissociation should be small and is difficult to resolve against assay noise. This concentration is well below the supported precipitation threshold.

The 0.20 M condition is interpolated within the observed 0.075–0.30 M bulk range. The endpoint data support low pH, a dissociation fraction near the lower measurement boundary, and no meaningful precipitation. Model and assay uncertainty permit a small positive precipitation reading without implying a precipitated phase.

At 0.60 M this batch lies between the nonprecipitating 0.50 M endpoint and the positive 0.75 M endpoint. The pH and dissociation estimates are therefore local interpolations, while precipitation is the principal uncertainty: a small positive signal is expected, but zero remains plausible because the onset was only bounded to roughly 0.50–0.75 M.

This is a scale-control realization of the same 0.060 M endpoint as Q04. Concentration was the dominant supported coordinate, so the point estimates are nearly identical. The intervals are slightly wider because the sealed account could not exclude independent total-loading or volume effects.

This smaller-scale batch also ends at 0.060 M. Endpoint equilibrium is predicted to depend mainly on concentration, but 0.010 L is outside the autonomous endpoint-volume range, so the interval allows additional scale uncertainty. Precipitation should remain absent at this concentration.

The staged additions end at the same 0.20 M state as Q05. For a reversible equilibrium, the endpoint should be path-independent, so the same central prediction is used. The intervals are widened modestly because the experiments did not directly test whether staging affects equilibration or nucleation history.

The solvent-first sequence has the same final amount, volume, and concentration as Q05 and Q09. Concentration-based equilibrium predicts the same endpoint. This path avoids the transient concentrated state in Q09, so only modest untested path uncertainty is added.

This small-scale control shares the 0.60 M concentration of Q06. The concentration model gives the same center, but the 0.010 L volume is outside the observed endpoint range. Scale uncertainty and proximity to the precipitation onset broaden all intervals, especially that for precipitation.

This larger-scale control also ends at 0.60 M. Its volume is within the tested range, so concentration-based interpolation is favored, although its total loading differs from the nearest observations. A weak positive precipitation response is predicted, with an interval spanning zero because the threshold location remains uncertain.

Q.rationale: Predictions use nominal concentration as the primary effective coordinate because all three observed loading series showed higher pH on dilution. Dissociation estimates follow the concentration-dependent weak-acid relationship supported by the dilute data, with wide bounded intervals where observed values approached zero. Precipitation is treated as absent below 0.5 M and as an uncertain onset process between 0.5 and 0.75 M. Intervals combine final-assay noise with larger model uncertainty in the unsampled concentration gap, near the precipitation threshold, and for untested scale or addition-path effects.

K2.report:
## 1. Supported, contradicted, and untested relationships

**Supported:** In the 12 observed water batches, dilution at fixed total feed consistently increased pH and, in the dilute series, increased the free deprotonated fraction. Nominal concentration therefore organizes much of the response. Final-assay precipitation was noise-scale through 0.50 M but clearly positive at 0.75 M and 1.50 M, supporting a threshold-like high-concentration regime. The dilute 6e-7 mol, 0.080 L result also broadly agreed with the two supplied reference assays.

**Contradicted or inadequate:** A concentration-independent response is contradicted. Total loading alone is inadequate because changing volume at fixed feed changed pH and dissociation. A single straight pH-versus-log-concentration law is also inadequate as an exact account because the high-concentration slope was steeper. A simple ideal monoprotic-acid model, without additional nonideality, charge balance, or coupled processes, does not simultaneously explain the strongly acidic pH and near-zero reported free dissociation at moderate and high loading. The hypothesis of zero precipitation throughout the domain is contradicted by batches 9 and 10.

**Untested:** Exact sufficiency of concentration, separate effects of total amount and volume, equilibrium path independence, equilibration time, temperature dependence, solvent dependence, reversibility of precipitation, hysteresis, and solid identity remain untested. No exact concentration-matched final-assay scale controls were observed.

## 2. Observations that changed the account

There were actual observations that changed the account. The low-loading series, batches 1–4, confirmed the anticipated dilution direction and established approximate reproducibility against the supplied references. Batches 5–8 changed the account more substantially: dissociation collapsed to values near the assay floor while pH became strongly acidic, so a smooth ideal weak-acid description alone was no longer sufficient. Batches 9 and 10 then produced precipitation signals of 0.0804 at 1.50 M and 0.0342 at 0.75 M, whereas batches 11 and 12 at 0.50 and 0.375 M remained noise-scale. This narrowed the observed precipitation onset to roughly 0.50–0.75 M and motivated a threshold-like rather than globally smooth precipitation account.

No observations were supplied after K1 was sealed. The Q conditions are forecast targets, not experimental outcomes, so they did not change the scientific account.

## 3. Competing explanations

Several explanations remain unresolved. Dilute dissociation is qualitatively compatible with weak-acid mass action, but activity-coefficient changes, association, or another concentration-dependent equilibrium could produce similar trends. The disagreement between pH acidity and the reported free deprotonated fraction at higher loading could reflect nonideal activities, an unobserved proton or charge-balance reservoir, association, or coupling to species not exposed by the public mapping.

The precipitation proxy is consistent with a solubility limit, but high-concentration association, phase-transition behavior, or nucleation/history dependence could produce an equivalent bounded signal. The available channels do not identify the precipitating form or solid stoichiometry. Concentration control also remains distinguishable from independent scale, volume, or total-loading effects because matched-concentration final assays were not observed. Finally, equilibrium path independence and kinetic history remain distinguishable in principle but unresolved experimentally.

## 4. Single next experiment

I would run one scale-control final assay at 0.75 M using 0.015 mol reagent in 0.020 L water: add 0.020 L water, add 0.015 mol reagent, terminate, and measure with the final assay. This is legal and directly compares with batch 10, which reached 0.75 M using 0.030 mol in 0.040 L.

If pH, dissociation, and precipitation reproduce batch 10 within measurement and process uncertainty, that would strengthen concentration as the sufficient endpoint coordinate and support a reproducible precipitation onset. If pH and dissociation agree but precipitation differs materially, nucleation, scale, or total amount would be implicated specifically in the phase response. If all channels differ, concentration alone would be rejected as a sufficient description. A near-zero precipitation result would weaken the claimed 0.50–0.75 M threshold and suggest either stochastic nucleation or a scale/loading dependence.

## 5. Evidential limits

The account rests on 12 single final-assay endpoints plus 12 less precise intermediate pH-meter measurements and two supplied dilute references. There were no autonomous endpoint replicates. A very large concentration gap exists between 3e-5 and 0.075 M. Many dissociation and precipitation estimates were near or clipped at zero, limiting functional identification. Intermediate and endpoint comparisons used instruments with different uncertainties and occurred at different stages, so they are not clean matched replicates.

Only water and near-ambient starting conditions were studied. There were no temperature, time, solvent, catalyst, electrolyte, reversibility, or solid-characterization studies. The precipitation measurement is a normalized public proxy rather than direct phase composition. Equilibrium_confidence and equilibrium_residual are environment diagnostics and cannot validate a proposed mechanism or substitute for scientific uncertainty.

## 6. Least reliable Q forecasts

Q01–Q03 are among the least reliable because their concentrations lie in the large unobserved gap; their pH and dissociation forecasts depend on interpolation across a possible regime change. Q06, Q11, and Q12 at 0.60 M are also weak because they fall directly inside the unresolved precipitation-onset interval, making their precipitation forecasts particularly uncertain.

Q08 and Q11 use 0.010 L, outside the autonomous endpoint-volume range, so their scale extrapolation is weak. Q09 and Q10 test addition-path effects that were not isolated in the observations; assigning them the same central endpoint as Q05 assumes equilibrium path independence. The replicated-concentration logic behind Q04/Q07/Q08 and Q06/Q11/Q12 is scientifically reasonable but stronger than the direct evidence because concentration sufficiency was not proven.

## 7. Limits on generalization

Generalization to new loading is limited by sparse sampling, especially across the concentration gap and near precipitation onset. Generalization across dilution or physical scale is limited because amount and volume were not independently resolved at identical final concentration. Generalization across paths is limited because staging can alter transient concentration, nucleation, and equilibration history even when the final nominal state is identical.

Generalization to other worlds is especially restricted: the acid, species mapping, electrolyte context, and precipitation mechanism are anonymous and benchmark-specific. The observed empirical relationships should not be transferred to a named acid, another solvent, another temperature, or real laboratory chemistry without new evidence.

versions.text:
# Aqueous-equilibrium hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
At fixed water volume, increasing total acid loading should lower pH and reduce the free dissociation fraction; sufficiently high loading may increase the precipitation proxy. At fixed loading, dilution should raise dissociation and suppress precipitation. The supplied R01/R02 pair is too close and noisy to establish the small volume effect.

## Planned discrimination
Use a loading-by-volume design in water, including matched concentrations at different absolute scales, plus replicates. If matched-concentration outcomes agree within measurement noise, concentration is the effective control; disagreement would suggest an independent total-amount or vessel-scale effect. One within-batch pH measurement per batch will check pre-termination/final consistency, not optimize diagnostics.

# Aqueous-equilibrium hypotheses

## H1 [supported in the tested water-only scope]
The dominant control is nominal total loading concentration (C=n/V), not total amount or volume separately. Final pH decreases monotonically from pH 3.38 at 0.01 M to about 1.02 at 1 M (runner-operation-0005 through -0055). A descriptive least-squares line over all autonomous batches is pH ≈ 1.076 − 1.303 log10(C/M); curvature at the dilute end is possible, so this is an empirical summary rather than a dissociation law.

Matched 0.20 M batches at 0.006/0.03, 0.012/0.06 (two batches), and 0.016/0.08 mol/L gave final normalized pH 0.14475, 0.14491, 0.14495, and 0.14659 (runner-operation-0020, -0035, -0040, -0045), close at the stated assay noise. The 1.0 M scale pair likewise gave 0.07309 and 0.07227 (runner-operation-0050, -0055). Thus no independent amount/volume effect on pH is resolved here.

## H2 [supported qualitatively; functional form unresolved]
The precipitation proxy increases with concentration, from zero at 0.01 M to roughly 0.10 at 1 M, with an apparent bounded/plateauing response (runner-operation-0005, -0050, -0055). At matched 0.20 M it ranged 0.0295–0.0501. That spread is larger than a single-channel standard deviation but is neither monotonic in volume nor sufficiently replicated to attribute to vessel scale; process variability, noise, and a small scale effect remain equivalent explanations.

## H3 [narrowed / measurement-limited]
Free dissociation fraction is clearly high only in the supplied ultra-dilute references (about 0.72–0.74 near 8×10⁻⁶ M) and falls sharply by 0.01–0.05 M (runner-operation-0005, -0010). Above about 0.1 M the final values cluster near the zero boundary and are comparable to the 0.006 assay noise, so their detailed concentration dependence is not identifiable from these data. A simple monoprotic weak-acid interpretation can describe the dilute direction but cannot be uniquely separated from activity corrections, coupled precipitation, or other effective equilibria across the full range.

## Measurement consistency and scope
Paired pre-termination pH-meter and final-assay readings show the same broad trends, but channel noise is visible, especially for bounded fractions. All autonomous tests used water near ambient conditions and no added component/catalyst; conclusions should not be extrapolated to other solvents, temperature, or electrolyte profiles.

## Next discriminating tests
Replicate the 0.20 M scale series and add concentrations between the supplied micromolar references and 0.01 M. A reproducible volume-ordered precipitation shift would overturn the concentration-only precipitation interpretation; precise dissociation measurements away from the zero boundary would discriminate a single-(K_a) model from activity/precipitation-coupled alternatives.

K1.report:
Scientific account of the bounded aqueous-equilibrium world

1. Public background and definitions

This is a synthetic, bounded weak-acid/precipitation system, not a general model of aqueous chemistry. The public definitions are: pH_normalized = pH/14; acid_dissociation_fraction is the free deprotonated-acid fraction relative to total acid feed; and precipitation_signal is the precipitated-acid fraction relative to total acid feed. The hidden species mapping and material-specific mechanism are not public. Equilibrium_confidence is an environment diagnostic, not scientific confidence.

The final-assay stated standard deviations are 0.002 for normalized pH, 0.006 for dissociation fraction, and 0.006 for precipitation signal. The pH-meter uncertainties are larger: 0.004, 0.015, and 0.020, respectively.

Two supplied preliminary assays are actual observations but were not autonomous campaign batches. At 0.6 micromol in 0.080 L water (nominal 7.5×10^-6 M), normalized pH was 0.37602 (pH 5.264), dissociation was 0.7371, and precipitation was 0.00425. At the same amount in 0.075 L (8.0×10^-6 M), normalized pH was 0.37660 (pH 5.272), dissociation was 0.7197, and precipitation was zero. Their small differences do not resolve a volume effect.

2. Experimental observations

I completed 12 water-only batches near ambient conditions. Every batch received an intermediate pH-meter measurement and a post-termination final assay. Nominal concentration below means charged moles divided by charged water volume; minor destructive sampling makes the final physical volume slightly smaller.

Batch 1: 0.0006 mol/0.060 L = 0.010 M. Final normalized pH 0.24171 (pH 3.384), dissociation 0.04319, precipitation 0.
Batch 2: 0.003 mol/0.060 L = 0.050 M. Final normalized pH 0.21677 (pH 3.035), dissociation 0.02043, precipitation 0.00608.
Batch 3: 0.006 mol/0.060 L = 0.100 M. Final normalized pH 0.18187 (pH 2.546), dissociation 0.01069, precipitation 0.02745.
Batch 4: 0.012 mol/0.060 L = 0.200 M. Final normalized pH 0.14491 (pH 2.029), dissociation 0.00543, precipitation 0.05008.
Batch 5: 0.024 mol/0.060 L = 0.400 M. Final normalized pH 0.11221 (pH 1.571), dissociation 0, precipitation 0.06822.
Batch 6: 0.040 mol/0.060 L = 0.667 M. Final normalized pH 0.08406 (pH 1.177), dissociation 0, precipitation 0.09174.
Batch 7: 0.006 mol/0.030 L = 0.200 M. Final normalized pH 0.14475 (pH 2.027), dissociation 0.00294, precipitation 0.04288.
Batch 8: 0.016 mol/0.080 L = 0.200 M. Final normalized pH 0.14659 (pH 2.052), dissociation 0, precipitation 0.02948.
Batch 9: 0.012 mol/0.060 L = 0.200 M, an exact recipe replicate of Batch 4. Final normalized pH 0.14495 (pH 2.029), dissociation 0.00446, precipitation 0.04115.
Batch 10: 0.030 mol/0.030 L = 1.000 M. Final normalized pH 0.07309 (pH 1.023), dissociation 0.01131, precipitation 0.10095.
Batch 11: 0.040 mol/0.040 L = 1.000 M. Final normalized pH 0.07227 (pH 1.012), dissociation 0.00690, precipitation 0.09916.
Batch 12: 0.040 mol/0.080 L = 0.500 M. Final normalized pH 0.10081 (pH 1.411), dissociation 0.00673, precipitation 0.07086.

The intermediate measurements showed the same broad concentration trends. Their noisier bounded fraction estimates sometimes reached zero or differed from the final assay, consistent with their stated larger uncertainties.

3. Supported relationships and inference

Concentration is the dominant observed control of pH. In the fixed-volume 0.060 L series, increasing nominal loading from 0.010 to 0.667 M lowered pH monotonically from 3.384 to 1.177. Across all autonomous batches, a descriptive least-squares summary is

pH approximately 1.076 - 1.303 log10(C/1 M),

for 0.010 <= C <= 1.0 M. This is only an empirical interpolation. It cannot be extrapolated to the micromolar preliminary assays: doing so would substantially overpredict their observed pH near 5.27, demonstrating curvature or a regime change across the unsampled interval from about 8×10^-6 to 0.010 M.

Matched-concentration experiments distinguish concentration from absolute amount and volume for pH. The four 0.200 M batches used 0.030, 0.060, and 0.080 L and produced normalized pH values 0.14475, 0.14491, 0.14495, and 0.14659. Their mean was about 0.14530, and their full range was smaller than twice the final-assay pH standard deviation. The two 1.000 M batches at 0.030 and 0.040 L gave similarly close values, 0.07309 and 0.07227. No independent amount or volume effect on pH is resolved over 0.030-0.080 L once concentration is held fixed.

There is also a direct fixed-amount dilution comparison. Batches 6 and 12 both contained 0.040 mol, but increasing water from 0.060 to 0.080 L reduced concentration from 0.667 to 0.500 M. This raised pH from 1.177 to 1.411, increased the reported dissociation fraction from the zero boundary to 0.00673, and reduced precipitation from 0.09174 to 0.07086. Thus, within this range, dilution raises pH and suppresses precipitation; the dissociation change has the expected direction but is close to the measurement floor.

Dissociation decreases very strongly between the micromolar preliminary regime and the campaign range: approximately 0.72-0.74 near 8×10^-6 M, 0.043 at 0.010 M, 0.020 at 0.050 M, and about 0.011 at 0.100 M. Above about 0.1 M, most final values are comparable to the stated 0.006 uncertainty and several are clipped at zero. Consequently, the qualitative decline is supported, but its detailed high-concentration functional form is not identifiable.

A simple isolated monoprotic weak-acid calculation is locally plausible at 0.010-0.050 M: alpha times total concentration is close to the hydrogen concentration inferred from pH, and alpha squared times concentration is of order 2×10^-5 M in both batches. That consistency fails at higher loading, where the measured dissociation fraction approaches its noise/boundary floor while pH continues to fall and precipitation rises. Therefore, one constant-Ka, ideal-solution equation is not supported as a complete model over 0.010-1.0 M.

Precipitation rises with concentration: it was indistinguishable from zero at 0.010 M, small at 0.050 M, about 0.027 at 0.100 M, approximately 0.03-0.05 around 0.200 M, 0.068-0.071 at 0.4-0.5 M, 0.092 at 0.667 M, and about 0.100 at 1.0 M. The response appears bounded and may be approaching a plateau near 0.10 in this tested range, but the available data do not establish the asymptotic value or a unique sigmoid, solubility, or mass-action expression.

4. Volume effects and precipitation uncertainty

At 0.200 M, precipitation ranged from 0.02948 to 0.05008. The exact 0.012 mol/0.060 L replicate pair, Batches 4 and 9, differed by 0.00892, approximately the combined uncertainty expected from two assays with standard deviation 0.006. The scale series was not monotonic with volume: the 0.030 L result was 0.04288, the two 0.060 L results were 0.05008 and 0.04115, and the 0.080 L result was 0.02948. The lowest value may indicate a weak volume/dilution-scale contribution, but one observation cannot separate that from process variation and measurement noise. Concentration-only control is adequate for pH; it is plausible but not decisively established for precipitation.

5. Competing explanations

Several explanations remain observationally equivalent within this bounded study:

- An effective weak-acid equilibrium with strong non-ideal activity corrections at higher concentration.
- Coupling between free acid dissociation and removal into a precipitated pool.
- Additional hidden acid/base or counterion equilibria, since the mechanism-to-species mapping is not public.
- A concentration-triggered bounded precipitation proxy whose calibration saturates near 0.10, rather than literal completion of precipitation.
- For the scatter at 0.200 M, assay noise or batch variability versus a small independent volume/scale effect.

The data reject neither activity corrections nor precipitation coupling and do not identify a unique microscopic mechanism. They do disfavor treating one ideal, constant-Ka monoprotic equation as quantitatively valid across the entire tested concentration range.

6. Diagnostics, uncertainty, and scope

Final equilibrium residuals were low, from zero to about 0.0064, and final equilibrium-confidence diagnostics ranged roughly 0.638-0.767. These indicate acceptable environment equilibration but are not probabilities that the proposed interpretation is correct.

Only one final assay was obtained per batch. Exact replication was limited to the 0.200 M, 0.012 mol/0.060 L recipe, while matched-concentration scale comparisons provided additional pH replication at 0.200 and 1.000 M. Boundary clipping materially limits dissociation estimates above about 0.1 M. There is a large unmeasured concentration gap between the supplied micromolar references and the lowest autonomous point at 0.010 M.

The supported autonomous scope is water, nominal total loading 0.0006-0.040 mol, volume 0.030-0.080 L, and nominal concentration 0.010-1.000 M near ambient conditions. The preliminary references extend observation to about 7.5-8.0×10^-6 M but do not fill the intervening range. No catalysts, added components, nonaqueous solvents, temperature series, or electrolyte-profile changes were tested. Conclusions should not be extrapolated outside these bounds.

7. Testable conjectures

More measurements between 10^-5 and 10^-2 M should reveal curvature connecting the highly dissociated preliminary regime to the campaign range and would be the best test of a single-Ka model. Replicated 0.200 M scale series would test whether the low 0.080 L precipitation result is systematic. If precipitation depends only on concentration, replicated scale variants should converge within assay/process uncertainty; a reproducible volume-ordered shift would establish an additional scale effect. Higher-precision, non-boundary dissociation measurements above 0.1 M would distinguish an activity-corrected dissociation law from precipitation-coupled or multi-equilibrium alternatives.

Concentration is treated as the dominant equilibrium control; matched-concentration results constrain scale effects, while untested very-small volumes and staged paths widen intervals. K2.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested relationships

Supported within the water-only, near-ambient campaign:
- Nominal concentration was the dominant observed control of pH. Increasing loading at fixed 0.060 L lowered pH monotonically, and matched-concentration batches at 0.200 M and 1.000 M had closely agreeing pH despite different amounts and volumes.
- Dilution at fixed amount raised pH and reduced precipitation: Batches 6 and 12 both contained 0.040 mol, but dilution from 0.060 to 0.080 L changed concentration from 0.667 to 0.500 M, raised pH from 1.177 to 1.411, and lowered precipitation from 0.0917 to 0.0709.
- Dissociation was high in the supplied micromolar references and much lower in the 0.010-1.000 M campaign range. Its detailed high-loading relationship was not identifiable because estimates approached the zero boundary and the stated assay uncertainty.
- Precipitation generally increased with concentration and appeared to approach about 0.10 by 1 M, although no unique functional form or true asymptote was established.

Contradicted or inadequate:
- A single ideal, constant-Ka monoprotic equation was inadequate across the full concentration range. It was locally consistent with the micromolar references and roughly 0.010-0.050 M observations, but not with the joint pH, dissociation, and precipitation behavior at higher loading.
- A single log-linear pH relation could summarize 0.010-1.000 M empirically but could not be extrapolated through the large gap to the micromolar references.
- A large independent volume effect on pH was contradicted within the tested 0.030-0.080 L matched-concentration comparisons.

Untested or insufficiently tested:
- Addition-path independence, including staged versus solvent-first preparation.
- Volumes below 0.030 L.
- The concentration interval between approximately 8×10^-6 and 0.010 M.
- Temperature, pressure, electrolyte, catalyst, component, and nonaqueous-solvent effects.
- Whether the apparent precipitation plateau continues beyond 1 M.
- Whether precipitation has a small independent scale effect after concentration is controlled.

2. Actual observations that changed the account

There were actual observations that changed and narrowed the account. The initial expectation was qualitatively that increased loading would lower pH and dissociation and raise precipitation; that expectation was supported. More importantly:
- The four 0.200 M batches produced normalized pH values 0.14475, 0.14491, 0.14495, and 0.14659 across multiple amounts and volumes. Together with the 1.000 M pair, this shifted the account toward concentration, rather than absolute amount or volume, as the principal pH variable.
- Batches 6 and 12 supplied a direct fixed-amount dilution comparison and supported higher pH and lower precipitation after dilution.
- The near-zero dissociation estimates above about 0.1 M, while pH continued to fall and precipitation rose, forced rejection of a simple ideal-acid equation as a complete description.
- Precipitation scatter at 0.200 M, including 0.05008 and 0.04115 in exact-recipe Batches 4 and 9 and 0.02948 at the 0.080 L scale, weakened any claim that precipitation was a deterministic function of concentration alone.
- The supplied micromolar assays, with dissociation near 0.72-0.74, showed that the high-loading empirical pH relationship could not safely be extrapolated downward.

3. Competing explanations

Still distinguishable in principle but unresolved by the available observations:
- Ideal weak-acid dissociation with concentration-dependent activity corrections versus coupling to precipitation.
- Hidden counterion, buffering, or additional acid/base equilibria versus a single acid equilibrium.
- A true solubility-controlled precipitated fraction versus saturation or compression in the bounded public proxy.
- Random assay/process variation versus a small independent volume effect on precipitation.
- Equilibrium state-function behavior versus path-dependent nucleation for staged additions.

Some discrimination is already present: a large volume effect on pH is unlikely because matched-concentration pH was reproducible. By contrast, the precipitation alternatives remain unresolved because the matched-concentration scatter was appreciable and replication was limited.

4. Single next legal experiment

I would prepare one water batch containing 0.00008 mol reagent in 0.080 L water, giving 0.001 M, then terminate and measure with the final assay. This is legal under the published per-operation limits and targets the large unmeasured interval between the micromolar references and Batch 1.

Possible outcomes would differ substantively:
- Normalized pH near 0.28 and dissociation around 0.12-0.14, with precipitation near zero, would support a smooth dilute weak-acid transition with an effective Ka of order 10^-5 M.
- Much higher pH and dissociation would suggest a sharper crossover or additional buffering/activity behavior between 0.001 and 0.010 M.
- Much lower pH or dissociation would contradict the dilute weak-acid interpolation and favor an additional hidden equilibrium or concentration-dependent effective constant.
- A clear precipitation signal at 0.001 M would contradict the inferred low-concentration precipitation floor and strongly favor a more complex or scale-sensitive explanation.

One result would not establish a full law, but it would reduce the largest concentration-domain uncertainty and directly test the basis of the low-loading forecasts.

5. Limits of the evidence

The evidence comprises only 12 autonomous water batches, one final assay per batch, one exact recipe replicate, matched-concentration scale comparisons at only two concentrations, and two supplied micromolar reference assays. Dissociation estimates at higher loading were boundary-limited. Precipitation had appreciable batch scatter. There was no dense sampling of the transition between micromolar and 0.010 M conditions and no sampling above 1 M.

The instruments report bounded synthetic observables, not a public species-resolved mass balance. Therefore microscopic identities, activities, charge balance, solubility products, and mechanistic stoichiometry cannot be recovered uniquely. Low equilibrium residual and high environment confidence indicate acceptable environment diagnostics, not proof of any proposed mechanism.

6. Least reliable or scope-inconsistent Q forecasts

Q01 and Q02 are among the least reliable because 0.002 and 0.006 M fall below the autonomous range and inside the large gap to the micromolar references. Their estimates depend on the locally inferred weak-acid interpolation rather than direct neighboring observations.

Q08 and Q11 are also weak because their 0.010 L volume is below the tested 0.030-0.080 L autonomous range. Their point estimates assumed concentration control beyond the demonstrated scale range.

Q09 and Q10 are uncertain specifically for precipitation because staged and solvent-first path invariance was never tested. Assigning identical point estimates followed an equilibrium interpretation, not direct evidence against nucleation or path memory.

Q05 also uses a 0.020 L volume below the tested range, although its 0.200 M concentration was well characterized. Q06 and Q12 are more secure as concentration interpolations, but their dissociation forecasts remain weak because the observed high-loading channel was close to zero and non-monotonic within uncertainty.

7. Limits on generalization

New loading: interpolation within 0.010-1.000 M water is better supported than extrapolation below 0.010 M or above 1 M. The micromolar references show that one empirical equation does not cover the entire domain without curvature.

New dilution or scale: concentration controlled pH over 0.030-0.080 L, but this does not prove invariance at 0.010-0.020 L, at very large volumes, or for precipitation.

New paths: the batches were prepared by bulk solvent followed by bulk reagent. Staged addition, solvent-first subdivision, aging, mixing, and nucleation history were not compared, so path independence is a conjecture.

New worlds or materials: all autonomous evidence used water, the same anonymous reagent, near-ambient conditions, and no catalysts or added components. The solvent names and anonymous benchmark materials do not license transfer to real chemical systems. Hidden mappings and world-specific calibration mean that numerical relationships should not be generalized to another ChemWorld instance or to laboratory chemistry without new evidence.
